newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says mining proposals negotiable.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says mining proposals negotiable.

text.p: Indonesia's director-general of mining said on Monday that proposed changes to mining regulations, including the requirement that foreign companies allocate a 10-percent stake free to the government, were negotiable.
"No, it's not a dead price," Adjat Sudradjat told reporters, using a local term referring to things that are not negotiable.
"There are about 17 points in the proposals ... it is mainly aimed at supervision so that there are no repeats of the Bre-X case," he said, referring to the country's biggest mining scandal.

Canadian exploration company Bre-X Minerals Ltd declared that its Busang property in East Kalimantan held some 71 million ounces of gold, which would have made it the biggest discovery this century. But an independent audit of Busang found it was almost worthless, and the data falsified on an unprecedented scale.

Sudradjat described the proposal to allocate a 10 percent stake to the government as minor and that it could be changed. "It is a small thing. What is more important is the (government) supervision," he said.
The government has given mining companies until Tuesday to respond to the proposals.
State Secretary Murdiono told reporters last Thursday the government would be consistent with its policy that allowed 100 percent foreign-owned companies to operate in the country.

Under the proposed changes, mining companies with operations in Indonesia are required to share capital gains made on stock exchanges outside the country with their shareholders. In addition, raising of additional capital through a public offering of shares must be done in Indonesia.
The government has informed mining companies similar changes will be made in the coal sector.
A copy of the proposed changes obtained by Reuters shows that coal companies must divest 51 percent of their equity in projects to Indonesians by the 10th year of operation.
